title: Slow and Rapid Changes to Earth's Surface
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Slow and Rapid Changes to Earth's Surface Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe how weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition cause slow or rapid change to Earth's surface (Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on slow and rapid changes to Earth's surface: earthquakes, landslides, floods, cyclones and slow weathering, with Australian examples. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Some changes take seconds, others millions of years.
key_sub: Earthquakes and landslides are fast; weathering and canyons are slow.
body_html:
How to think about it

Earth's surface changes all the time, some quickly and some very slowly.

  • Rapid changes take seconds to days: earthquakes, landslides, floods, storm surges, volcanic eruptions.
  • Slow changes take years to millions of years: weathering, rivers carving gorges, dunes moving, mountains wearing down.
  • People cannot stop natural hazards, but they can reduce the damage with warnings, stronger buildings and careful planning.
Example

Thredbo, 1997: a hillside slid in seconds. Fast or slow?

it happened in seconds

Answer: fast (a landslide)

Example

A river makes a gorge. How long?

the water wears away rock a little at a time

Answer: thousands to millions of years

Common mistakes

  • Thinking that big changes are always slow.
  • Thinking people can stop earthquakes or cyclones.
  • Mixing up the cause of a change (rock slipping underground) with its effect (cracked roads).

faq.q: What are some rapid changes to Earth's surface?
faq.a: Earthquakes, landslides, floods, tsunamis, storm surges during cyclones and volcanic eruptions can change the land in seconds, hours or days.

faq.q: Why does Australia have so few earthquakes and volcanoes?
faq.a: Australia is in the middle of a large plate of rock, far from the edges where most earthquakes and volcanoes happen. Small earthquakes still happen, such as the Newcastle earthquake in 1989.

faq.q: How do people reduce damage from natural hazards?
faq.a: They use warning systems, build stronger buildings, avoid building on flood plains and steep loose slopes, and keep sand dunes covered with plants.

items.q: What is a natural hazard?
c: a natural event that can harm people or property
items.e: Earthquakes, floods and cyclones are natural hazards.

items.q: Noah compares roots cracking a rock and a flood. Which happens slower?
items.e: Roots cracking a rock takes many years; a flood takes hours or days.

items.q: Is a tsunami a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: A tsunami takes minutes to hours.

items.q: Why can a cyclone change a beach quickly?
c: Strong winds push big waves that carry away sand.
items.e: Storm surges cause rapid erosion.

items.q: Is wind wearing down a rock a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: Wind wearing down a rock takes thousands of years.

items.q: Which kind of change made most of Australia's landforms, such as Uluru?
c: slow weathering and erosion over millions of years
items.e: Australia's landscape is very old and worn down.

items.q: Is a volcanic eruption a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: A volcanic eruption takes hours to days.

items.q: Jack compares a flood and waves wearing away a cliff. Which happens faster?
items.e: A flood takes hours or days; waves wearing away a cliff takes hundreds of years.

items.q: Mei compares a river carving a canyon and an earthquake. Which happens slower?
items.e: A river carving a canyon takes millions of years; an earthquake takes seconds or minutes.

items.q: Jack compares a storm wave hitting a dune and a river carving a canyon. Which happens faster?
c: a storm wave hitting a dune
items.e: A storm wave hitting a dune takes hours; a river carving a canyon takes millions of years.

items.q: Is water dissolving a limestone cave a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: Water dissolving a limestone cave takes thousands of years.

items.q: Is tree roots cracking a rock a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: Tree roots cracking a rock takes many years.

items.q: Which of these is the effect of an earthquake, not its cause?
c: moving plates of rock deep underground
items.e: The cause is underground; the effect is what we see.

items.q: Which of these changes Earth's surface slowest?
items.e: This takes millions of years.

items.q: Is a sand dune moving inland a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: A sand dune moving inland takes many years.

items.q: Is a landslide a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: A landslide takes minutes.

items.q: Which of these changes Earth's surface fastest?
items.e: A landslide can happen in minutes.

items.q: Can people stop earthquakes from happening?
c: No, but they can build stronger buildings to reduce damage.
items.e: We can plan for hazards but not stop them.

items.q: Is mud building up at a river mouth a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: Mud building up at a river mouth takes hundreds of years.

items.q: Is a sinkhole opening a fast change or a slow change to Earth's surface?
c: a change only in the air
items.e: A sinkhole opening takes minutes.

items.q: Chloe finds a video of lava pouring down a volcano in one night. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in one night.

items.q: Harper finds a photo of a town flooded the day after a big storm. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in one day.

items.q: About how long does a tsunami take to change the land?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: Chloe finds a book that says the canyon took millions of years to form. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: Millions of years is very slow.

items.q: Why are landslides more likely after very heavy rain?
c: Water makes the soil heavy and slippery.
items.e: Wet soil slides more easily.

items.q: About how long does a sand dune moving inland take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: About how long does a mountain range wearing down take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Ethan finds photos of a cliff taken 50 years apart that look almost the same. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: The cliff barely changed in 50 years.

items.q: Aarav finds a chart showing a beach losing a little sand each year for 100 years. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: A little each year for 100 years.

items.q: How can a flood change the land quickly?
c: It erodes soil and drops mud in new places.
items.e: Floods cause both erosion and deposition.

items.q: William finds a video of mud sliding over a road in 1 minute. Is this evidence of a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It happened in 1 minute.

items.q: Chloe looks at this picture. This volcano erupts. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: About how long does a flash flood take to change the land?
items.e: It is a fast change.

items.q: About how long does mud building up at a river mouth take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: About how long does a river carving a gorge take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: About how long does waves wearing back a cliff take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Priya looks at this picture. This storm floods a town. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes hours or days.

items.q: About how long does water dissolving a limestone cave take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: Ruby looks at this picture. Wind and rain wear down this mountain. Is it a fast change or a slow change?
items.e: It takes millions of years.

items.q: About how long does wind wearing down a rock take to change the land?
items.e: It is a slow change.

items.q: What does a levee do?
c: holds back river water to protect land from floods
items.e: A levee is a wall of soil or concrete along a river.

items.q: What is a constraint for a flood solution?
c: It must keep water out of homes.
It must cost less than the town can spend.
items.e: Constraints are limits like money, time and materials.

items.q: How does a volcanic eruption change Earth's surface?
c: It covers the land with lava and ash.
It cracks the ground and can make buildings fall.
It drops boulders at the bottom of the cliff.
items.e: A volcanic eruption covers the land with lava and ash.

items.q: How does a mountain range wearing down change Earth's surface?
c: It smooths and shapes the rock.
It floods the coast and carries away sand.
It makes the mountains lower and rounder.
items.e: A mountain range wearing down makes the mountains lower and rounder.

items.q: What is a criterion for a flood solution?
c: It must keep water out of homes.
It must take 100 years to build.
items.e: Criteria tell what the solution must do.

items.q: In 1974 Cyclone Tracy hit Darwin with very strong winds and big waves. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: How does a river carving a gorge change Earth's surface?
c: It breaks the rock into pieces.
It floods the coast and carries away sand.
It moves soil and rock down a slope.
items.e: A river carving a gorge makes a deep valley.

items.q: How does wind wearing down a rock change Earth's surface?
c: It washes away beaches and sand dunes.
It drops boulders at the bottom of the cliff.
It breaks the rock into pieces.
It smooths and shapes the rock.
items.e: Wind wearing down a rock smooths and shapes the rock.

items.q: In 2022 heavy rain made the Wilsons River rise quickly and cover the streets of Lismore. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: In 1997 a hillside above Thredbo village slid down in a few seconds after water soaked the soil. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: In 1989 the ground shook in Newcastle, New South Wales, and buildings were damaged in seconds. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: What is a natural hazard?
c: a natural Earth process that can harm people, like an earthquake or flood
items.e: Earthquakes, floods, tsunamis, volcanoes and landslides are natural hazards.

items.q: How does tree roots cracking a rock change Earth's surface?
c: It cracks the ground and can make buildings fall.
It breaks the rock into pieces.
It drops boulders at the bottom of the cliff.
It washes away soil and leaves mud behind.
items.e: Tree roots cracking a rock breaks the rock into pieces.

items.q: How does a landslide change Earth's surface?
c: It moves soil and rock down a slope.
It floods the coast and carries away sand.
It drops boulders at the bottom of the cliff.
It buries the land behind it.
items.e: A landslide moves soil and rock down a slope.

items.q: In 2011 Brisbane River water rose and covered many suburbs in mud. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: What should you do during an earthquake inside a building?
items.e: Get under a sturdy table and hold on.

items.q: How does water dissolving a limestone cave change Earth's surface?
c: It cracks the ground and can make buildings fall.
It washes away beaches and sand dunes.
It makes caves and tunnels underground.
items.e: Water dissolving a limestone cave makes caves and tunnels underground.

items.q: How does a storm surge in a cyclone change Earth's surface?
c: It makes new land at the coast.
It buries the land behind it.
It makes caves and tunnels underground.
It washes away beaches and sand dunes.
items.e: A storm surge in a cyclone washes away beaches and sand dunes.

items.q: In 2016 huge storm waves washed away sand and parts of backyards at Collaroy Beach. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: Rocks often break off the sandstone cliffs at Sydney's beaches and land on the rocks below. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.

items.q: A town uses this plan: bolting houses to their foundations. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of earthquakes.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from landslides?
c: flexible gas pipes that bend instead of breaking
tsunami warning buoys in the ocean
sensors that detect moving ground on hillsides
tower shelters on the beach that rise above giant waves
items.e: Sensors that detect moving ground on hillsides helps protect people from landslides.

items.q: Does Australia have active volcanoes on the mainland today?
c: No. The last eruptions on the mainland were thousands of years ago.
items.e: Mount Gambier and Tower Hill erupted thousands of years ago.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from floods?
c: tsunami warning buoys in the ocean
building storm drains to carry water away
planting trees and grass on steep slopes
measuring small earthquakes and gases near the volcano to warn people
items.e: Building storm drains to carry water away helps protect people from floods.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from earthquakes?
c: channels that guide mudflows away from towns
not building homes in the path of old lava flows
dust masks to protect from falling ash
building with flexible frames and steel supports
items.e: Building with flexible frames and steel supports helps protect people from earthquakes.

items.q: A town uses this plan: nets that catch falling rocks. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of landslides.

items.q: A town uses this plan: piling sandbags along a riverbank. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of floods.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from volcanic eruptions?
c: flexible gas pipes that bend instead of breaking
not building homes on low land next to rivers
channels that guide mudflows away from towns
items.e: Channels that guide mudflows away from towns helps protect people from volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from earthquakes?
c: flood gates that close when the river rises
pumps that move water out of low streets
items.e: Bolting houses to their foundations helps protect people from earthquakes.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from floods?
c: not building houses at the bottom of steep, loose slopes
tower shelters on the beach that rise above giant waves
dust masks to protect from falling ash
items.e: Raising houses on stilts helps protect people from floods.

items.q: What causes most tsunamis?
items.e: A sudden movement of the sea floor pushes up a huge wave.

items.q: A town uses this plan: dust masks to protect from falling ash. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Can people stop earthquakes from happening?
c: No, but they can reduce the damage.
items.e: We cannot stop Earth's processes, but we can prepare.

items.q: A town uses this plan: practising “drop, cover and hold on” drills. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of earthquakes.

items.q: A town uses this plan: building retaining walls. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of landslides.

items.q: A town uses this plan: planting mangrove forests along the shore to slow giant waves. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of tsunamis.

items.q: A town uses this plan: sensors that detect moving ground on hillsides. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of landslides.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from volcanic eruptions?
c: not building houses at the bottom of steep, loose slopes
planting trees and grass on steep slopes
items.e: Evacuation plans for nearby towns helps protect people from volcanic eruptions.

items.q: Which solution would best reduce damage from tsunamis?
c: dust masks to protect from falling ash
marked evacuation routes to high ground
not building homes on low land next to rivers
pumps that move water out of low streets
items.e: Marked evacuation routes to high ground helps protect people from tsunamis.

items.q: A town uses this plan: tower shelters on the beach that rise above giant waves. Which hazard is it mainly designed for?
items.e: This solution reduces the impact of tsunamis.

items.q: Mia compares two photos of a cliff taken 60 years apart. The cliff has moved back 3 m. How much did it move each 20 years, on average?
items.e: 3 m ÷ 3 = 1 m each 20 years. This is a slow change.

items.q: Zara's photo from 1950 and her photo from today show the same cliff, almost the same. What kind of change is the cliff having?
items.e: Very little change in many years.

items.q: A town near the ocean has a tsunami warning siren but no marked path to high ground. What would improve the plan most?
c: build more houses on the beach
mark evacuation routes to high ground
items.e: People need to know where to go after the warning.

items.q: Ella makes a model hill of wet sand and dry sand. She pours the same water on both. What is she testing?
c: whether wet soil slides more easily
items.e: The variable is how wet the sand is.

items.q: Sienna compares a flood and a river carving a canyon. Which happens slower?
items.e: A river carving a canyon takes millions of years; a flood takes hours or days.

items.q: Kai wants evidence that a beach is wearing away. Which source helps most?
c: photos of the beach taken every year for 20 years
items.e: Photos over time show slow change.

items.q: Ruby compares roots cracking a rock and a rock falling off a cliff. Which happens faster?
c: a rock falling off a cliff
items.e: A rock falling off a cliff takes seconds; roots cracking a rock takes many years.

items.q: Jack shakes a tray with two model buildings. One is tall and thin, one is short and wide. Which is more likely to fall?
items.e: A wide base is more stable.

items.q: Which solution helps both people near volcanoes and people near rivers?
items.e: Evacuation plans help with many hazards.

items.q: Kai compares a landslide and a rock wearing into sand. Which happens faster?
items.e: A landslide takes minutes; a rock wearing into sand takes thousands of years.

items.q: Amelia compares a river carving a canyon and a landslide. Which happens faster?
items.e: A landslide takes minutes; a river carving a canyon takes millions of years.

items.q: Mia reads that a landslide covered a road in 2 minutes. Which word fits?
items.e: 2 minutes is fast.

items.q: Why might a town choose wetlands instead of a concrete wall to reduce floods?
c: Wetlands soak up water and give homes to wildlife.
items.e: Different solutions have different benefits.

items.q: Ruby compares a landslide and a river carving a canyon. Which happens slower?
items.e: A river carving a canyon takes millions of years; a landslide takes minutes.

items.q: A town measures how high the river rises during a storm every 30 minutes. What can this data help them do?
items.e: Data helps plan for hazards.

items.q: Which evidence shows a slow change to the land?
c: rock layers worn down over thousands of years
a news report about an earthquake
photos of a landslide on a road
items.e: Slow changes need evidence from long times.

items.q: Scientists put sensors on a hill that is slowly moving. Why?
c: to warn people if the movement speeds up
items.e: Monitoring helps reduce harm.

items.q: Mia compares two earthquake solutions. One costs less but protects less. What should she consider?
c: how much protection the town needs and how much it can spend
items.e: Compare solutions using criteria and constraints.

items.q: Lachlan tests two model levees with a cup of water. Levee A leaks; levee B holds. What should he do next?
c: test levee B again to be sure the result repeats
items.e: Repeated tests show the design is reliable.

items.q: Mount Gambier in South Australia formed when hot, melted rock came out of the ground thousands of years ago. What kind of event was this?
items.e: This was a rapid change to Earth's surface.
